advances: Ordinary marked convex bodies and actual compact convex fibers with full-dimensional interior marks. The result is an energy interpolation statement without a mixed halfspace-depth estimate.

proof:
Omit zero weights. Interior balls about the retained $y_i$ combine to give an interior ball about $y$ in $M$. Write $E_i=E_{K_i}(y_i)$ and let $L_i$ be its attained positive affine denominator. By the attainment and escort lemma, $\rho_i=L_i^{-d-2}/E_i$ is a positive continuous density on $K_i$, of mass one, barycenter $y_i$, and mean denominator one.

**Conditional quantiles.** Fix orthonormal coordinates. For a density $\rho$ of this form on a convex body $K$, let $m_j$ be the first $j$ coordinate marginal density, integrating $\rho\mathbf1_K$ over the remaining coordinates, with $m_0=1$ and $m_d=\rho\mathbf1_K$. These are Borel functions. Let $P_j$ be the projection of $\operatorname{int}K$ onto the first $j$ coordinates, with $P_0$ the singleton empty prefix. For $j<d$, a prefix $p\in P_j$ has a full-dimensional slice in the remaining coordinates because it is the projection of an interior point. The interior of that slice consists of points coming from $\operatorname{int}K$. Indeed, a supporting normal at a purported boundary point in the slice interior would vanish in the remaining directions and would then support the prefix projection at the interior point $p$. When prefixes converge to $p$, membership eventually holds at every interior point of the limiting slice, and eventually fails outside the closed limiting slice by closedness of $K$. Its boundary has zero volume. Dominated convergence in a fixed box, using boundedness and continuity of the density on $K$, gives continuity of $m_j$ on $P_j$, and the full-dimensional slice gives positivity. For $j=d$ these properties follow directly from those of $\rho$.

For a prefix $p\in P_{j-1}$, the next coordinate ranges over a bounded open interval in $P_j$. Its closed counterpart is the section of the closed $j$-coordinate projection, since a convex combination with positive weight on an interior prefix lift approaches each endpoint from inside that interval. Thus $m_j(p,t)$ vanishes off this interval except possibly at its endpoints. The conditional CDF
$$
F_j(p,t)=\frac{\int_{-\infty}^{t}m_j(p,s)\,ds}{m_{j-1}(p)}
$$
rises continuously and strictly from zero to one there by positivity and Fubini. Its inverse $q_j(p,u_j)$ for $0<u_j<1$ is Borel since $q_j(p,u_j)<t$ is equivalent to $u_j<F_j(p,t)$. Define $X_j$ recursively as $q_j(X_{<j},u_j)$ on the uniform cube $(0,1)^d$. The resulting bounded Borel map $X$ is triangular, and its image is $\operatorname{int}K$ because each point there is recovered by taking its own conditional CDF values. For fixed earlier input coordinates its $j$-th coordinate is $C^1$ and strictly increasing in $u_j$, with derivative $b_j=m_{j-1}(X_{<j})/m_j(X_{\le j})>0$. These factors telescope to $J_X:=\prod_j b_j=1/\rho(X)$.

The general triangular substitution proved in accepted fact f6641f09c19819a3 applies to any bounded Borel triangular map $T$ on the cube with $C^1$ increasing own-coordinate maps and strictly positive own-coordinate derivatives. It gives a Borel image $U_T$ and inverse there by recursive interval inversion, and successive one-dimensional substitutions give the pushforward density $J_T(T^{-1}(x))^{-1}$ on $U_T$, where $J_T$ is the product of those derivatives. Equivalently, $\int_{U_T} G(x)\,dx=\int_{(0,1)^d}G(T(u))J_T(u)\,du$ for nonnegative Borel $G$ by using the density formula with $G(x)J_T(T^{-1}(x))$ on $U_T$. In particular each $X_i$ constructed for $\rho_i$ pushes cube measure to $\rho_i\,dx$. The weighted average $S=\sum_i\lambda_i X_i$ is bounded and Borel, with triangular own-coordinate derivatives $\sum_i\lambda_i b_{ij}>0$ that are continuous in their current coordinate. The same substitution therefore applies to $S$, with image $U_S\subset M$.

**Inequality.** At each cube point, finite Hölder gives
$$
J_S=\prod_j\Big(\sum_i\lambda_i b_{ij}\Big)
\ \ge\ \Big(\sum_i\lambda_i(\prod_j b_{ij})^{1/d}\Big)^d.
$$
Put $A=\sum_i\lambda_i E_i^{1/d}$, $w_i=\lambda_i E_i^{1/d}/A$, and $\bar L=\sum_iw_iL_i(X_i)$. Substituting $\prod_j b_{ij}=E_i L_i(X_i)^{d+2}$ and using convexity of $s\mapsto s^{(d+2)/d}$ gives $J_S\ge A^d\bar L^{d+2}$. The cube means of $S$ and $\bar L$ are $y$ and $1$, respectively. For any parameter $a$ admissible on $M$, write $B=1+a\cdot(S-y)$. It is positive with cube mean one. Inclusion of $U_S$ in $M$, triangular substitution, and Hölder on the cube give
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_M [1+a\cdot(x-y)]^{-d-1}\,dx
&\ge\int_{(0,1)^d} J_S B^{-d-1}\,du\\
&\ge A^d\int_{(0,1)^d}\bar L^{d+2}B^{-d-1}\,du
\ \ge\ A^d.
\end{aligned}
$$
For the last step, apply Hölder to $\bar L=(\bar L B^{-(d+1)/(d+2)})B^{(d+1)/(d+2)}$ using the cube means of $\bar L$ and $B$. The estimate for every admissible $a$ proves the lower bound.

**Equality.** Use the attained target parameter on $M$. Equality forces equality almost everywhere in both the diagonal product inequality and the power convexity step, since their pointwise gaps are nonnegative and the integral weights are positive. Strict convexity of the power gives $L_i(X_i)=L_1(X_1)$ for every retained $i$ almost everywhere. To obtain the equality case of the diagonal product inequality, normalize its columns by setting $p_{ij}=\lambda_i b_{ij}/\sum_\ell\lambda_\ell b_{\ell j}$. Its proof is $\sum_i(\prod_j p_{ij})^{1/d}\le d^{-1}\sum_{ij}p_{ij}=1$ by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality in each row. For $d\ge2$, equality requires every row to be constant across the columns. It follows that $b_{ij}/b_{1j}$ is independent of $j$. Taking products and using the equality of denominators identifies this ratio as $c_i=(E_i/E_1)^{1/d}$. For $d=1$ the product identity and equal denominators already give the same ratio.

Repeat the construction with any unit vector $e$ as the first coordinate. The first coordinates of the escort maps are quantiles of the one-dimensional projections onto $e$ and depend only on $u_1$. Their derivatives satisfy $X'_{i,1}=c_i X'_{1,1}$ almost everywhere by Fubini. They are $C^1$ on $(0,1)$, so $X_{i,1}=c_i X_{1,1}+b_i(e)$ throughout that interval. Taking their means gives $b_i(e)=e\cdot y_i-c_i e\cdot y_1$. Taking the upper endpoint limits gives $h_{K_i-y_i}(e)=c_i h_{K_1-y_1}(e)$, where $h_K(e)=\max_{x\in K}e\cdot x$. Indeed the positive escort density gives positive marginal density on the whole interior of the projection interval, so its upper quantile limit is the actual support endpoint. This holds in every direction, and compact convex sets are determined by their support functions.

Conversely, if $K_i-y_i=c_i(K_1-y_1)$ for positive $c_i$, then $M-y=(\sum_i\lambda_i c_i)(K_1-y_1)$ by convexity. Affine covariance of energy gives equality. For distinct marks on the same body, volume forces the homothety factor to be one, and equality of centered bodies would then give a nonzero translation preserving a bounded set. This proves strict fixed-body concavity. The containing-body statement follows by inclusion monotonicity, with strictness for proper inclusion. For fibers, convexity of $C$ gives $\sum_i\lambda_i C_{z_i}\subset C_{\sum_i\lambda_i z_i}$. An interior ball about the combined mark in the Minkowski sum certifies its membership in the joint domain and the containing-body bound proves concavity there.
statement:
Let $d,m\ge1$, let $K_i\subset\mathbb R^d$ be convex bodies, and choose $y_i\in\operatorname{int}K_i$ and weights $\lambda_i\ge0$ with $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$. Use the energy $E_K(y)=\min_{a:\,1+a\cdot(x-y)>0\ (x\in K)}\int_K[1+a\cdot(x-y)]^{-d-1}\,dx$. Put $M=\sum_i\lambda_i K_i$ and $y=\sum_i\lambda_i y_i$. Then $y\in\operatorname{int}M$ and
$$
E_M(y)^{1/d}\ \ge\ \sum_i\lambda_i E_{K_i}(y_i)^{1/d}.
$$
Equality holds exactly when the centered bodies $K_i-y_i$ with $\lambda_i>0$ are positive scalar multiples of one another. In particular $y\mapsto E_K(y)^{1/d}$ is strictly concave on $\operatorname{int}K$.

If $H$ is a convex body containing $M$, the same lower bound holds for $E_H(y)^{1/d}$. Equality then requires both $H=M$ and the same marked homothety condition. Consequently, for a compact convex set $C\subset\mathbb R^{n+d}$ with fibers $C_z=\{x:(z,x)\in C\}$, the function $(z,y)\mapsto E_{C_z}(y)^{1/d}$ is jointly concave on the convex domain $\{(z,y): y\in\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^d}C_z\}$.
title: Joint Minkowski concavity and marked homothety for projective volume energy
